The core revenue metrics investors use to price businesses
• Annualized value of recurring software contracts active at a point in time • In private cloud markets, ARR is the primary metric used to determine valuation
• Signed but not yet live contracts which capture near-term pipeline visibility • Especially useful in long implementation cycles, often a better indicator of revenue growth rather than ARR alone

• The growth rate of ARR matters almost as much as the absolute size or level of ARR itself • Investors pay higher multiples for higher sustained growth • Growth is a proxy for product-market fit, sales efficiency, and market leadership
• Why do recurring revenue metrics matter for the performance evaluation of SaaS companies?
• Since these companies operate on a subscription model, recurring revenue is the best indicator of their size and growth.
• To ensure consistency, it is typically reported on a monthly or annual basis, depending on the most common contract length among customers.
ARR (Annual Recurring Revenue) MRR (Monthly Recurring Revenue)

• Represents the recurring revenue from all subscription contracts, normalized on a monthly basis • MRR is always equal to one-twelfth of Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) • One-time revenues are excluded to maintain a clear and consistent measure of predictable income

• Represents the recurring revenue from all subscription contracts, normalized on an annual basis • ARR is always equal to 12 times Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) • One-time revenues are excluded to maintain a clear and consistent measure of predictable income, as for MRR
➢ In practice, ARR is calculated as the previous month's MRR multiplied by 12
Retained ARR Recurring revenue that continues from existing customers from the previous period
Contraction ARR Recurring revenue lost due to customers downgrading their contracts from the previous period
New Sales ARR Recurring revenue acquired from new customers in the current period
Churned ARR Recurring revenue lost as a result of customers fully cancelling their contracts from the previous period
Resurrected ARR Recurring revenue regained from former customers who have re-subscribed
Expansion ARR Additional recurring revenue generated from existing customers compared to the previous period (Cross- or Upselling)
Recurring Revenue at the Account or User Level
Average Revenue Per Account: Measures the average recurring revenue per customer account. It can be reported monthly, quarterly, or annually ARPR ARPU
Average Revenue Per User: Similar to ARPA but calculates revenue per individual user, considering that one account may have multiple users. In consumer software, ARPA and ARPU are often the same
How ARR growth rate and endurance shape valuation, risk, and long-term scalability ARR Growth & Growth Endurance
• It shows stable, repeatable income, not only one-time sales
ARR Growth = Year-over-Year % increase in recurring revenue
? Why this matters: Higher ARR growth reduces investor risk faster and drives higher valuations, as investors pay more today when they expect ARR to double or triple soon.

• Company A makes 10M ARR and investors value it at $200M • Their valuation is at 20x ARR →expensive • If Company A now grows 100% it will have $20M ARR • At the same valuation of $200M, investors then paid only 10x ARR instead of the 20x
• It shows how much of the growth rate the company “kept” compared to last year and how sticky is their momentum
• On average, public cloud companies, keep about 80% of their growth rate from one year to the next.
Growth Endurance = Current Year Growth ÷ Prior Year Growth
• YoY: 150% → 120% → 96% → 77% • Because small differences in endurance create huge differences over time.
? Why this matters: Strong growth endurance sustains investor confidence and supports higher valuations, as investors pay more for businesses that can compound ARR consistently over time.
• 80% E → $100M ARR In 6 years • 70% E → $100M ARR In 12 years
Why S&M stays high Salespeople and marketing talent scale linearly with revenue - unlike R&D or G&A, you cannot get away with fewer sales reps as you grow.
What Matters High S&M must be justified by ARR generated. S&M efficiency = capital efficiency. Without it, no rational burn rate is possible.
Case Study Adaptive Insights spent ~90% of revenue on S&M at <$20M ARR. Even when acquired by Workday in 2018 at $100M+ ARR, S&M was still ~70% of revenue.
All average benchmarks across 5 ARR buckets — Bessemer Venture Partner's cloud portfolio 2010–2021
CAC Payback: The Sales Efficiency Indicator
CAC Payback = Prior Quarter S&M Expense ÷ (Net New MRR × Gross Margin)
Segment Targets: SMB < 12 months · Mid-Market < 18 months · Enterprise < 24 months
CLTV / CAC Rule: Invest in customer acquisition only when CLTV/CAC ≥ 3x. Below that, refine unit economics first. Only after payback period expires do customers become profitable.

Why it increases at scale: Early adopters are cheapest to acquire. As you mature, you compete for harder-to-win customers with more spend. But $100M+ companies unlock proven GTM models that justify the cost.
Free Cash Flow Margin: Burn with Purpose
Tracks how much cash a company burns relative to revenue — and whether that burn is justified by the growth it generates.
FCF Margin = Free Cash Flow ÷ Revenue | FCF = Revenue − COGS − OpEx − CapEx + Non-Cash − ΔNWC
← Burn Decreases as ARR Scales → (Path to FCF Breakeven)
Top Quartile at IPO : Best-in-class companies, Atlassian, JFrog, Zoom, were already at FCF breakeven (0%+) at IPO. This signals strong capital discipline and operating leverage.

The Snowflake Exception : Snowflake burned >$100M at IPO but grew revenue by $170M+ (>170% YoY). When growth justifies the burn, high FCF deficit is accepted. Growth > Profitability — at the right stage.
The Efficiency Score sums ARR growth and FCF margin
Efficiency Score = FCF Margin (%) + ARR YoY Growth Rate (%)
Only meaningful at $25M+ ARR, below that, revenue base too small for the ratio to be reliable
Even at $3.8bn+ LTM revenue, Shopify still hits ~70% efficiency score: 60% YoY growth + 10% FCF margins (Proof that category leaders sustain elite efficiency at massive scale)
• $25 - 50M ARR: Target 70% efficiency score • $100M+ ARR: Target 50% (growth rate declines, focus shifts to profitability balance)
Tracks how much ARR a company generates per dollar of net capital deployed and what growth-stage investors are willing to pay for it
Cash Conversion Score (CCS) ARR Valuation Multiples
Data Infra Zapier: Best-in-Class CCS Raised only $1.3M total — announced $140M ARR in 2021. CCS far exceeds 1.0x. Proof that capital efficiency compounds.
Round Size & Dilution: More Capital, Less Ownership Sold
As ARR proves itself, companies raise larger rounds, but give away less equity per dollar, because valuation grows faster than capital needs
Dilution falls ~20% → ~5% (valuation grows faster than capital
ARR buckets grow non-linearly (10x from $10M → $100M), but round sizes increase only linearly ($30M → $75M). Larger companies are not
raising proportionally bigger rounds, so access to capital gets easier, but discipline over dilution is rewarded.
What is preferred stock and how does it differ from common? Q1:
How does a 2x liquidation preference work on a $1M investment? Q2:

• A 2x liquidation preference means the investor must receive 2x their invested capital before common shareholders receive any proceeds. (e.g. on a $1M investment, the investor is entitled to $2M first at exit)

• Preferred stock is a class of equity that has priority over common shares in the event of a liquidation or exit. • Unlike common shareholders, preferred investors typically have a liquidation preference, meaning they recover their investment (often a multiple) before common shareholders receive anything.
• Non-participating preferred: investor takes either the $2M preference or converts to common and shares pro-rata.
• Preferred shares are usually convertible into common, allowing investors to participate in upside if the company performs well.
• Participating preferred: investor takes the $2M preference and shares the remaining proceeds pro-rata with common.
Key Insight: GE norm is non-participating preferred, less punitive to founders. Participating preferred is more common in earlier-stage VC deals.
Mechanisms designed to protect investors from ownership dilution and unwanted cap table changes
What is the difference between a right of first refusal (ROFR) and a co-sale agreement? Q1:
What is the difference between a full ratchet provision and a weighted average provision? Q2:
• A ROFR gives investors the right to purchase a founder's shares before they can be sold to an outside party, allowing them to prevent unwanted third parties from entering the cap table

• A full ratchet provision protects early investors and their preferred ownership stakes in the case of a down-round • An investor will be re-priced to the lowest price at which any new preferred stock is issued
• A co-sale agreement gives investors the right to sell their shares alongside the founder on the same terms, allowing them to exit at the same time and price
• The weighted average provision also adjusts the conversion price in a down round, but factors in the size of the new issuance, resulting in a fairer, less severe dilution.
• The key difference is the goal: ROFR is about blocking outside buyers, while a co-sale agreement is about joining a sale
Key Insight: ROFR and co-sale control who can sell and to whom, while anti-dilution provisions protect the value of what investors already own.
Understanding how funding rounds affect company valuation and ownership stakes
What is the difference between an up round and a down round? Q1:
When could dilution be beneficial for the founder and existing investors? Q2:
• Dilution can be beneficial when it occurs in an up round:
• Up Round: when post-financing, the valuation of the company raising additional capital increases compared to its previous valuation
• A founder owns 100% of a startup worth $5M. In the seed round, the company is valued at $20M and angel investors take 20% of the company
• Down Round: refers to when the valuation of a company decreases after the financing round
• The founder's stake drops from 100% to 80%, but their actual value grows from $5M to $16M
• A smaller slice of a much bigger pie is worth more than a larger slice of a smaller one
Key Insight: Dilution is not always negative, what matters is not the size of your stake, but the value behind it
Why is vertical SaaS often attractive for GE? Q2:
What defines horizontal SaaS and what are its tradeoffs? Q1:
• Targets one function across all industries (e.g. Salesforce for CRM). • Huge TAM but fierce competition and high S&M spend. • Churn can be higher, buyers have more alternatives.

• Purpose-built for one industry (e.g. Veeva for pharma, Toast for restaurants). • Lower churn: deeply embedded in industry workflows, high switching costs. • Need credible second-act expansion story to justify venture-scale valuation.
Key Insight: Vertical SaaS tends to have more efficient CAC and higher NRR, but is there a real expansion path in vertical Sass beyond the core market?
What do you assess about the team itself? Q1:
What strategic questions do you ask management? Q2:

• Have they scaled through this exact stage before? Track record matters. • Is the org complete , meaning CFO, VP Sales, VP Engineering all in seat? • Are they the right people to take this to IPO or acquisition?

• 3–5 year financial targets and the assumptions behind them. • Where is growth being left on the table, white space, new geos, adjacent products? • Top 2–3 revenue drivers, biggest risk to each, and exact use of proceeds.
Key Insight: The best management diligence question: 'What would have to be true for you to miss your plan?’ →it reveals assumptions & self-awareness
How is GE structurally safer than VC or PE? Q1:
What contractual protections does GE rely on? Q2:
• Preferred equity + liquidation preference: capital recovery priority. • Anti-dilution provisions: protection against down rounds. • Redemption rights: exit mechanism if company stalls indefinitely.

• vs. VC: invests in proven revenue — far less binary, no productmarket fit bet. • vs. PE: zero leverage, so no debt service spiral risk in a downturn. • Minority stakes keep founders incentivized; no forced operational overhaul.
Key Insight: Sweet spot: floor is higher than VC (no zero outcomes from pre-revenue bets), ceiling is higher than PE (no leverage cap on returns). The risk profile is genuinely distinct.
How would you compute Revenue from the ARR? Q1:
What is preferred stock and how does it differ from common?
1 Gather Beginning ARR The annualized value of all active recurring contracts at the start of the period. Beginning ARR
2 Build the ARR Bridge Track all movements during the period: new logos signed, expansions/upsells, churned customers, and contractions/downgrades.
Beg. ARR + New Logos + Expansions − Churn − Contractions
3 Derive Ending ARR Sum all ARR bridge components to get the ARR at end of period (e.g., Dec 31). Ending ARR = Beg. ARR ± Net Changes

4 Compute Monthly ARR (MRR) Build Divide each month's ARR snapshot by 12 to get the MRR earned that month. New ARR added mid-month contributes only a partial month. MRR (Month n) = ARR at start of Month n ÷ 12
5 Sum MRR Across All Months Add up recognized MRR for each month in the period. This is the most precise method. Revenue = Σ MRR (Month 1 through Month 12)
6 Quick Approximation For back-of-envelope math, use the simple average of Beginning and Ending ARR. This works because ARR changes roughly linearly. Revenue ≈ (Beg. ARR + End. ARR) ÷ 2
Key Insight: In fast-growing SaaS companies, revenue understates ARR, which is why investors anchor valuations on forward ARR or NTM revenue multiples rather than LTM revenue.
